extracted.intended_audience: students and philosophers of logic; scientists and methodologists interested in the foundations of induction and demonstration
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and conceptual standards for judging when and how inductive inferences can be legitimately drawn, how inductions combine to yield deductions, and how sciences become deductive. Focuses on 'marks', chains of reasoning, and the status of mathematical/deductive truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of general reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: "The principle of general reasoning ... is, that if, from observation of certain known particulars, what was seen to be true of them can be inferred to be true of any others, it may be inferred of all others which are of a certain description."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as the core test for applying an induction: determine the 'certain description' (distinguishing marks) that authorizes carrying an observed property from known particulars to unobserved cases. The real premises are the individual observations even when summarized by a general proposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: General propositions as formulaic guides (not intermediate premises)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The successive general propositions are not steps in the reasoning, are not intermediate links in the chain of inference, between the particulars observed and those to which we apply the observation. ... They are mere formulæ for inferring particulars from particulars."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat stated generalizations as schema that record the criteria used in past inductions. They guide whether an induction should be applied to a new case but are not themselves the original empirical premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination and recognition of distinguishing marks
rubrics_metrics.description: "In order that we may never fail to draw this conclusion in a new case when it can be drawn correctly, and may avoid drawing it when it can not, we determine once for all what are the distinguishing marks by which such cases may be recognized."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To apply induction correctly, identify the marks that make a new case fall under a previous induction. Marks may be recognized directly or via other marks (marks of marks); failure to identify correct marks is an anti-pattern leading to invalid induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks-of-marks and chained recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: "These marks we either recognize at once, or by the aid of other marks, which by another previous induction we collected to be marks of the first. Even these marks of marks may only be recognized through a third set of marks; and we may have a train of reasoning, of any length, to bring a new case within the scope of an induction..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept multi-step indirect identification: a new case may be brought under an induction by repeatedly identifying intermediate marks. Explicitly document each intermediate mark and the induction that justifies treating it as a mark of the next.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining multiple chains of induction
rubrics_metrics.description: "They consist ... of several chains united at the extremity, as thus: a a mark of d, b of e, c of f, d e f of n, therefore a b c a mark of n."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex inferences often require combining separate inductions whose conclusions jointly serve as marks for a further induction. The method: establish each chain to its terminal marks, then show the joint terminal marks warrant the final inference (example: parabolic reflector case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulæ for inferring equality and inequality (geometrical exemplars)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists the primitive formulæ used to infer equality and inequality (e.g., 'Things which being applied to each other coincide, are equals'; 'Things which are equal to the same thing are equals'; and for inequality: 'A whole and its parts are unequals', etc.). In the Euclidean reconstruction six specific formulæ are used: 1) The sums of equals are equal. 2) Equal straight lines or angles, being applied to one another, coincide. 3) Straight lines, having their extremities coincident, coincide. 4) Angles, having their sides coincident, coincide. 5) Things which coincide are equal. 6) The differences of equals are equal."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attempting to derive a property (e.g., equality of base angles), map the case onto one or more of these primitive formulæ by finding suitable auxiliary constructions. The difficulty often lies in selecting pairs or combinations that make the target fall under a known formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between experimental and deductive sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: "A science is experimental, in proportion as every new case ... stands in need of a new set of observations and experiments—a fresh induction. It is deductive, in proportion as it can draw conclusions ... by processes which bring those cases under old inductions; by ascertaining that cases which cannot be observed to have the requisite marks, have, however, marks of those marks."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evaluate whether a field is deductive or experimental, check whether generalizations are connected by identified marks-of-marks enabling indirect inference. A field with many isolated generalizations remains experimental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation of sciences via connecting generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: "A new set of instances, and a consequent new induction, may at any time bridge over the interval between two of these unconnected arches; b, for example, may be ascertained to be a mark of c, which enables us thenceforth to prove deductively that a is a mark of c."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that discovery of linkages (marks that connect previously detached generalizations) can convert parts of an experimental science into deductive subsystems. Look for comprehensive inductions (e.g., Newton) that unify many isolated laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics (science of number) as a universal tool for deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: "The grand agent for transforming experimental into deductive sciences, is the science of number. The properties of number, alone among all known phenomena, are, in the most rigorous sense, properties of all things whatever..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When variations of quality correspond regularly to quantitative relations, mathematical theorems provide intermediate 'marks' enabling deductive inference. Seek algebraic or numerical representations that map qualities to quantities to render phenomena amenable to deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status of geometric definitions and the 'necessity' of mathematical truths
rubrics_metrics.description: "The conclusions of geometry are deduced, partly at least, from the so-called Definitions ... There exist no points without magnitude ... To get rid of this difficulty ... it is customary to say that the points, lines, circles, and squares which are the subject of geometry, exist in our conceptions merely ... I conceive [Dugald Stewart's] doctrine ... that it is built on hypotheses."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat mathematical 'necessity' as conditional: conclusions are necessarily true only relative to the hypotheses (idealizing definitions) adopted. Do not mistake formal necessity (following from assumptions) for empirical necessity. When evaluating mathematical claims applied to the world, check the adequacy of the idealizing hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical convenience of idealization and the need for correction when irregularities matter
rubrics_metrics.description: "There exist no real things exactly conformable to the definitions of geometry ... When we have occasion to extend these inductions ... to cases in which the error would be appreciable ... we correct our conclusions, by combining with them a fresh set of propositions relating to the aberration ..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use idealizations (definitions that ignore small irregularities) for convenience but explicitly account for corrections when deviations from idealized assumptions are non-negligible. Document what properties are neglected and supply propositions or corrections addressing their effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of ingenuity in producing deductive demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: "The difficulty ... is chiefly that of figuring to ourselves the two angles ... as remainders made by cutting one pair of angles out of another ... It is by this happy contrivance that so many different inductions are brought to bear upon the same particular case ... how much scope there may well be for scientific dexterity ..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proofs and demonstrations not only on logical validity but on the ingenuity of constructions that bring a new case under known formulæ. Pay attention to auxiliary constructions or choices (e.g., selecting particular angle pairs) that enable chaining inductions.
